summary.text: Take \(k=31\), \(s=1\), and the distinct integers \(5\) and \(1829=31\cdot59\). Their divisor sums coincide: \(1/32+1/36=17/288\), while \(1/32+1/62+1/90+1/1860=17/288\), so they have the same fractional part.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
S_{k,s}(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}\frac{1}{(d+k)^s},
\]
where the sum is over the positive divisors of the positive integer \(n\). The conjecture asserts, in particular, that for every pair of positive integers \(k,s\), the fractional parts of the numbers \(S_{k,s}(n)\) are pairwise distinct as \(n\) ranges over the positive integers.

We disprove this by taking
\[
k=31,\qquad s=1,
\]
and comparing the two distinct positive indices
\[
n_1=5,\qquad n_2=1829.
\]

First determine their divisors. Since \(5\) is prime, its positive divisors are exactly
\[
1,5.
\]
Also,
\[
1829=31\cdot 59.
\]
Both factors are prime: \(31\) has no prime divisor among \(2,3,5\), the primes not exceeding \(\sqrt{31}\), and \(59\) has no prime divisor among \(2,3,5,7\), the primes not exceeding \(\sqrt{59}\). Since \(31\) and \(59\) are distinct primes, the positive divisors of \(1829\) are therefore exactly
\[
1,31,59,31\cdot59=1829.
\]

For \(n=5\), the sum is consequently
\[
\begin{aligned}
S_{31,1}(5)
  &=\frac1{1+31}+\frac1{5+31}\\
  &=\frac1{32}+\frac1{36}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Putting these terms over the common denominator \(288\) gives
\[
S_{31,1}(5)=\frac9{288}+\frac8{288}=\frac{17}{288}.
\]

For \(n=1829\), using its four positive divisors gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
S_{31,1}(1829)
 &=\frac1{1+31}+\frac1{31+31}+\frac1{59+31}+\frac1{1829+31}\\
 &=\frac1{32}+\frac1{62}+\frac1{90}+\frac1{1860}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The last three terms combine to \(1/36\). Indeed, \(5580\) is a common denominator and
\[
\frac1{62}+\frac1{90}+\frac1{1860}
 =\frac{90}{5580}+\frac{62}{5580}+\frac3{5580}
 =\frac{155}{5580}
 =\frac1{36}.
\]
It follows that
\[
S_{31,1}(1829)=\frac1{32}+\frac1{36}=\frac{17}{288}.
\]
Thus
\[
S_{31,1}(5)=S_{31,1}(1829).
\]
In particular, their fractional parts are equal. More explicitly, since
\(0<17/288<1\), each fractional part is exactly \(17/288\):
\[
\operatorname{frac}(S_{31,1}(5))
 =\frac{17}{288}
 =\operatorname{frac}(S_{31,1}(1829)).
\]

The indices \(5\) and \(1829\) are positive and unequal, while \(k=31\) and \(s=1\) are also positive. Hence this is a direct violation of the claimed pairwise distinctness of fractional parts. The conjecture requires both pairwise distinctness and nonintegrality for every positive \(k,s\); failure of the pairwise-distinctness clause for this one choice of \(k,s\) is enough to disprove the entire conjecture.
